summary.text: A 37-year-old man with inactive untreated Hepatitis B, prior intermittent hematuria and painful D-J intolerance had prolonged bilateral obstructing calculi (right UVJ 8/9 mm, left UPJ 12.6 mm) and grade 2 hydronephrosis. Preoperative culture was negative and hemoglobin 18.3 g/dL.

Initial semirigid endoscopic stone treatment is described as right-sided and later bilateral ureterolithotripsy lasting 40 minutes. Bilateral 4.8 Fr 28 cm D-J stents were inserted without initial problems or fluoroscopy/contrast. Day 1 bilateral pain, worse left, and hematuria prompted KUB demonstrating left proximal protrusion. Reposition under local anesthesia failed to form a loop, leading to suspected extrarenal position and complete left-stent removal.

Symptoms persisted through day 3, worsening with mobilization. Day 4 severe hematuria prompted bladder irrigation then triphasic CTA showing left nutcracker renal vein syndrome. Authors linked renal injury to this syndrome and possible guidewire force; mechanisms and pressure were unmeasured. Bed rest, NSAI, IV hydration and source-literal cefuroxime axetil 2 x 500 mgIV were provided. Renal damage was reported without perirenal hematoma or urinoma.

During conservative follow-up, no left flank pain or transfusion need was reported; the exact observation time is unstated. On postoperative day 5, hemoglobin was 14.9 g/dL and mild hematuria with right flank pain persisted. Repeat cystoscopy under spinal anesthesia found bleeding hyperemic bladder-neck areas, treated with bipolar fulguration; neither ureteric orifice showed bloody efflux. The right stent was removed and right diagnostic URS found only small calcular fragments and tissue debris, without other pathology or bleeding focus. A 22 Fr three-way urethral catheter was inserted.

Symptoms regressed after cystoscopy/right-stent withdrawal, discharge home occurred on postoperative day 7, and later outpatient visits disclosed no clinical problems; follow-up duration is unreported.

summary.text: A 30-year-old man without reported comorbidity had a 9.3 mm right upper ureter stone with grade 2 hydronephrosis and over 2 months obstruction. Preoperative urine culture showed no bacterial growth. During 20-minute URS the stone was pushed proximally, preventing laser lithotripsy; a 4.8 Fr 28 cm right D-J was inserted over a 0.035-inch hydrophilic sensor guidewire without initial problems, fluoroscopy or contrast.

Severe right flank pain and hematuria developed that evening. Same-day KUB raised suspicion of upper-calyx rotation and injury; authors reported renal parenchymal damage without hematoma/urinoma. Bed rest, NSAI and IV hydration were used; the abstract also reports antibiotherapy with no case-specific drug details. Possible excessive guidewire force remains an author hypothesis.

Day 1 worsening symptoms did not fully respond to IV dexketoprofen 2 x 50 mg and IM pethidine hydrochloride 2 x 50 mg. Right-stent extraction under local anesthesia reduced symptoms. Day 2 hematuria resolved completely but pain worsened again. CT after removal showed right grade 3 hydroureteronephrosis, UV junction edema and 35 mm renal pelvis AP diameter. The discussion separately claims CT stent malposition; that contradictory timing remains unresolved.

Day 2 repeat right diagnostic URS found UV edema without other pathology; the D-J was reinserted with the same guidewire type, gentle handling and real-time fluoroscopy confirming its proximal loop in the right renal pelvis. Pain/hematuria improved. Day 3 KUB confirmed position before discharge; later outpatient visits showed no clinical problems, with duration unspecified.
